title: Top-p Sampling: Why the Same Setting Keeps 2 Tokens One Time and 8 the Next
excerpt: Same top-p setting, 2 candidate tokens or 8: see how the cutoff follows the shape of the probabilities.

headings.text: What the Wider Pool Lets In
Why the Toy Vocabulary Understates the Risk

html:
A language model writes text one token at a time (a token is a word or a piece of a word). At each step it gives every possible next token a probability, then picks one at random, weighted by those probabilities. That weighted random pick is called sampling. Top-k sampling limits the pick to a fixed number of the highest-probability tokens. That's predictable, but it ignores whether the model is sure or spread across many options.

Top-p sampling, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, where p is a number you choose, such as 0.90 for 90%. ("Nucleus" just means the core group of likely tokens.) When one or two tokens dominate, that group is tiny. When the probabilities are spread out, the group widens. This post shows it on a small made-up vocabulary of 12 candidate answers, with code you can rerun.

The Rule

Sort the probabilities from highest to lowest and add them up in order, keeping a running total. Stop at the first token where the total reaches p. Keep everything up to that point (call it the pool), drop the rest, and rescale the kept probabilities so they add up to 100% again. For example, if the top two probabilities are 76.69% and 15.48%, the running total is 76.69%, then 92.17%. With p=0.90 the rule stops at the second token, so the pool is two tokens.

def top_p_filter(probs, p):
    idx_sorted = np.argsort(probs)[::-1]
    cumulative = np.cumsum(probs[idx_sorted])
    cutoff = np.searchsorted(cumulative, p) + 1  # smallest n with cumulative >= p
    kept_idx = idx_sorted[:cutoff]
    kept_probs = probs[kept_idx]
    return kept_idx, kept_probs / kept_probs.sum(), cumulative[cutoff - 1]

Why stop at the first token that crosses p instead of the one just before it? Because the rule promises the pool covers at least p. On the T=2.0 distribution below, the first seven tokens add up to only about 88.7%, so the eighth is needed to get past 90%.

The toy question is: "How many days do I have to recover a deleted file?" The correct answer is 30. The vocabulary has eight wrong-but-believable numbers (14, 90, 60, 45, 7, 10, 365, 0) and three words that don't answer the question at all (immediately, never, unsure). Each token starts with a hand-picked raw score, called a logit. Softmax, the formula that turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 1, converts them. Temperature (T) is a dial applied before softmax: a low T makes the top choice dominate (a sharp distribution), and a high T makes the probabilities more similar (a flat one). Every number below comes from running the code.

Same p, Three Different Pools

Is the rule doing something different at each temperature? No. It is the same p=0.90 and the same code; only the shape of the probabilities changes. Here, temperature is simply the dial that makes the distribution sharper or flatter.

  • T=0.5 (sharp): the pool is 2 tokens, 30 and 14, together covering 92.17% of the probability. The sampler (the step that picks the next token) never considers the other ten.
  • T=1.0: the pool is 4 tokens, 30, 14, 90, and 60, covering 92.76%.
  • T=2.0 (flat): the pool is 8 tokens, 30, 14, 90, 60, 45, 7, 10, and 365, covering 91.74%.

The T=1.0 pool is a subset of the T=2.0 pool, because temperature changes how spread out the probabilities are but not their ranking. In this example the pool size follows how flat the distribution is.

For contrast, top-k with k=4 keeps 4 tokens every time, but the share of the probability it covers moves with the shape: 99.65% at T=0.5, 92.76% at T=1.0, and only 72.24% at T=2.0. Top-p holds that coverage near 92% by letting the pool size change instead.

What the Wider Pool Lets In

Does a wider pool mean the model starts saying nonsense? Not on this toy vocabulary: none of the three words that don't answer the question enter any of the three pools. That is a feature of this example, not a guarantee.

The wrong numbers are another matter. 14 is already in the T=0.5 pool, 90 and 60 join at T=1.0, and the T=2.0 pool adds 7, 10, and 365. Every pool beyond the single top token holds believable wrong answers, and the wider pool holds more of them. This post does not compute how often each would be drawn.

So the trade-off is real. A tight pool keeps the generated text close to the model's top choice, which makes it more predictable. A wider pool gives the model room to vary, and that room includes more wrong-but-plausible options. Top-p doesn't decide which side you want; it lets you tune how much of the unlikely end of the list you're willing to draw from.

Why the Toy Vocabulary Understates the Risk

If the pool adapts this well, why not set p once and forget it? A real model chooses among tens of thousands of tokens, not twelve. Its unlikely end (the long tail of tiny probabilities) can be crowded, and when the distribution is flat the running total may need many of those tiny entries to reach p. That would pull many low-quality tokens into the pool even though no single one looks likely. This toy example does not demonstrate that; treat it as the reason to test p on your own model, not as a measured result.

Top-p is adaptive (the pool size adjusts automatically), but adaptive does not mean safe: it only guarantees that the kept tokens cover at least p of the total probability, not that they are correct.

Get the Code

The softmax, temperature, and top-p filter, with the T=0.5, T=1.0, and T=2.0 pools and the fixed-k comparison: TopPSampling.py.

Summary

Top-p keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p. On the same toy vocabulary with p=0.90, the pool was 2 tokens at T=0.5, 4 at T=1.0, and 8 at T=2.0, each covering about 92% of the total probability. A fixed top-k of 4 covered 99.65%, 92.76%, and 72.24% of it on the same three distributions. So top-p's pool size follows how spread out the probabilities are, while top-k's does not. The adaptation is not a safety guarantee: a wider pool admits more plausible-looking wrong answers, and on a real vocabulary the unlikely end of the list may matter more than it does here.
